The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

derivations.claim:
Put $c=2\pi\epsilon>0$ and define $D_cg(\xi)=c^{-d/2}g(\xi/c)$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$. A null set is sent to a null set by the same change-of-variables theorem [F2], so this definition is independent of the representative of $g$. Apply [F2] to $T(\eta)=c\eta$, whose Jacobian determinant is $c^d$, and to the nonnegative function $f(\xi)=|g(\xi/c)|^2$. This gives
$$ \|D_cg\|_2^2=c^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}|g(\xi/c)|^2\,d\xi =c^{-d}c^d\int_{\mathbb R^d}|g(\eta)|^2\,d\eta =\|g\|_2^2. $$
The inverse is $D_{1/c}$, as direct substitution shows, so $D_c$ is unitary.

By [F3], $\mathcal F_\epsilon u=D_c\mathcal F_2u$ for every $u\in\mathcal S$. Both factors extend unitarily by step 1.1 and [F1], so their composition is a unitary extension to $L^2$. Since $\mathcal S$ is dense and the extension is continuous, no other continuous extension can differ on any $L^2$ vector.

derivations.claim: Set $q=(x+y)/2$ and $r=x-y$. Then $x=q+r/2$, $y=q-r/2$, and the absolute Jacobian of $(q,r)\mapsto(x,y)$ is $1$. In these coordinates, $$ K_\epsilon(q,r)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a(q,\xi)\,d\xi=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}(\mathcal F_\epsilon^{-1}a(q,\cdot))(r). $$ Applying [F2] to the $\xi$-section for each $q$, then [F3] to integrate the resulting nonnegative function in $q$, gives $$ \|K_\epsilon\|_2^2=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}|a(q,\xi)|^2\,d\xi\,dq=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\|a\|_2^2. $$ Thus $K_\epsilon\in L^2(\mathbb R^{2d})$ with the asserted norm.

For $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^d)$, the section $K_\epsilon(x,\cdot)$ lies in $L^2$ for almost every $x$ by [F3]. For those $x$, define $(A_\epsilon u)(x)=\int K_\epsilon(x,y)u(y)\,dy$. Cauchy–Schwarz in the Hilbert space pairing [F4] gives $$ |A_\epsilon u(x)|^2\leq\left(\int|K_\epsilon(x,y)|^2\,dy\right)\|u\|_2^2. $$ Integrating in $x$ and using [F3] shows $A_\epsilon u\in L^2$ and $\|A_\epsilon u\|_2\leq\|K_\epsilon\|_2\|u\|_2$. For $u\in\mathcal S$, the kernel formula defining $A_\epsilon u$ is exactly [F1], so this is the required bounded extension.

The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. $$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$

and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

derivations.claim: For $Z=(q,p)$, define the normalized Gaussian packet $$ g_Z^\epsilon(x):=(\pi\epsilon)^{-d/4}e^{-|x-q|^2/(2\epsilon)}e^{ip\cdot(x-q/2)/\epsilon}. $$ Its norm is $1$ by [F3] at zero after the change of scale $x-q=\sqrt{\epsilon/2}\,s$. For $u\in\mathcal S$, put $V_\epsilon u(Z)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\langle u,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle$. The Fourier transform of the shifted Gaussian gives $$ \langle u,g_{q,p}^\epsilon\rangle=(\pi\epsilon)^{-d/4}e^{ip\cdot q/(2\epsilon)}(2\pi\epsilon)^{d/2}\mathcal F_\epsilon\!\left(u(\,\cdot\,)e^{-|\cdot-q|^2/(2\epsilon)}\right)(p). $$ Plancherel [F2], followed by Tonelli [F4] and $\int e^{-|x-q|^2/\epsilon}\,dq=(\pi\epsilon)^{d/2}$, gives $$ \|V_\epsilon u\|_2^2=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int|\langle u,g_{q,p}^\epsilon\rangle|^2\,dq\,dp=(\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int\!\!\int |u(x)|^2e^{-|x-q|^2/\epsilon}\,dx\,dq=\|u\|_2^2. $$ The middle equality follows from Plancherel [F2] for each fixed $q$; the final equality is the Gaussian integral [F3] in $q$, with Tonelli [F4]. The same identity holds for all $u\in L^2$ by [F2] and Tonelli [F4]. Polarization gives $\langle u,v\rangle=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int\langle u,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle\overline{\langle v,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle}\,dZ$, hence the weak resolution $$ u=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}\langle u,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle g_Z^\epsilon\,dZ . $$

For $u\in\mathcal S$, the joint function $F(x,q):=u(x)e^{-|x-q|^2/(2\epsilon)}$ is Schwartz in $(x,q)$: each derivative is a finite sum of derivatives of $u$, Gaussian factors, and polynomials in $x-q$, and the inequality $\langle q\rangle^m\le C_m\langle x\rangle^m\langle x-q\rangle^m$ transfers every $q$-weight to a Schwartz factor and a Gaussian moment. Its partial Fourier transform in $x$ is Schwartz in $(p,q)$ by the same full Fourier/inverse Fourier argument as [F8]. The additional phase $e^{ip\cdot q/(2\epsilon)}$ in $\langle u,g_{q,p}^\epsilon\rangle$ has derivatives that are polynomial factors, so the packet coefficient $V_\epsilon u$ remains Schwartz in $Z=(q,p)$. The Schwartz seminorms of $Z\mapsto g_Z^\epsilon$ grow at most polynomially in $Z$, so the resolution integral in step 1.1 converges in every Schwartz seminorm. The product $u(x+y/2)\overline{v(x-y/2)}$ is Schwartz in $(x,y)$; its partial Fourier transform is Schwartz by [F8], so $\mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v]\in\mathcal S$ and $|B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)|\le\|a\|_\infty\|\mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v]\|_1$ proves continuity of the form in Schwartz seminorms. If $a\in\mathcal S$, its Weyl kernel is Schwartz; the kernel pairing is absolutely convergent, and the change $q=(x+y)/2,\ r=x-y$, followed by $r\mapsto-y$, identifies it with $B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)$. Thus the bounded-symbol form extends the kernel definition on Schwartz symbols. Applying the continuous form to the two Schwartz-convergent resolutions is valid; Fubini [F5] for the resulting absolutely integrable products gives $$ B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\iint B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'}^\epsilon,g_Z^\epsilon)V_\epsilon u(Z')\overline{V_\epsilon v(Z)}\,dZ'\,dZ . $$

Let $Z=(q,p)$, $Z'=(q',p')$, $m=(Z+Z')/2$, and $\delta=Z-Z'$. Define $\sigma((x,\xi),(x',\xi'))=x\cdot\xi'-\xi\cdot x'$. Substitution of the packets into $\mathcal W_\epsilon[g_{Z'}^\epsilon,g_Z^\epsilon]$, completing the square in $y$, and applying [F3] gives $$ \mathcal W_\epsilon[g_{Z'}^\epsilon,g_Z^\epsilon](z)=(\pi\epsilon)^{-d}e^{-|w|^2/\epsilon}e^{-i\sigma(w,\delta)/\epsilon+i	heta(Z,Z')},\qquad w=z-m, $$ with $|e^{i	heta(Z,Z')}|=1$. If $|\delta|\leq\sqrt\epsilon$, its $L^1$ norm is $1$, hence $|B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'},g_Z)|\leq\|a\|_\infty$. If $|\delta|>\sqrt\epsilon$, then $$ L_\delta:= rac{\epsilon}{i|\delta|^2}
abla_w\phi_\delta\cdot
abla_w,\qquad \phi_\delta(w):=-\sigma(w,\delta) $$ satisfies $L_\delta e^{i\phi_\delta(w)/\epsilon}=e^{i\phi_\delta(w)/\epsilon}$, since $|
abla_w\phi_\delta|=|\delta|$. Integrating by parts $N_d$ times against the Gaussian, and scaling $w=\sqrt\epsilon\,s$, shows that every derivative on the Gaussian contributes a factor bounded by $\sqrt\epsilon/|\delta|$; a derivative on $a$ contributes $\epsilon/|\delta|\leq\sqrt\epsilon/|\delta|$, since $|\delta|>\sqrt\epsilon$ and $\epsilon\leq1$. Thus $$ |B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'},g_Z)|\leq C_d\left(\sum_{|\alpha|\leq N_d}\epsilon^{|\alpha|/2}\|\partial^\alpha a\|_\inftyight)(1+|\delta|/\sqrt\epsilon)^{-N_d}\leq C_dD(a)(1+|Z-Z'|/\sqrt\epsilon)^{-N_d}, $$ where $D(a)=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq N_d}\|\partial^\alpha a\|_\infty$. Increasing $C_d$ makes this bound valid also when $|\delta|\leq\sqrt\epsilon$.

Partition $\mathbb R^{2d}$ into cubes of side $\sqrt\epsilon$. For each fixed $Z$, the sum of $(1+|Z-Z'|/\sqrt\epsilon)^{-N_d}$ over these cubes, each weighted by its volume $\epsilon^d$, is at most $C_d\epsilon^d\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^{2d}}(1+|k|)^{-N_d}\leq C_d'\epsilon^d$, since $N_d=4d+4>2d$. The same holds with $Z,Z'$ interchanged. Thus the integral kernel $$ K_\epsilon(Z,Z'):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'}^\epsilon,g_Z^\epsilon) $$ has uniformly bounded row and column $L^1$ norms, each at most $C_dD(a)$. For $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^{2d})$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\int K_\epsilon(Z,Z')f(Z')\,dZ'|^2\leq(\int|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')|\,dZ')\int|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')||f(Z')|^2\,dZ'$. Integrating in $Z$ and using the column bound yields $\|K_\epsilon f\|_2\leq C_dD(a)\|f\|_2$. Applying this estimate to step 2.1 and using the isometry in step 1.1 proves $$ |B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)|\leq C_dD(a)\|V_\epsilon u\|_2\|V_\epsilon v\|_2=C_dD(a)\|u\|_2\|v\|_2 . $$

For fixed $u\in\mathcal S$, the bounded form in step 3.1 extends continuously in $v$ to $L^2$, which is a Hilbert space by [F6], and $v\mapsto\overline{B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)}$ is a bounded linear functional there. Its norm is at most $C_dD(a)\|u\|_2$. Uniqueness makes $u\mapsto A_\epsilon u$ linear on $\mathcal S$, and this bound extends it uniquely to $L^2$. Hence the operator norm is at most $C_dD(a)$.

Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

derivations.claim: Let $\widehat a(\lambda)=\int e^{-i\lambda\cdot z}a(z)\,dz$, and similarly for $b$. These are rescaled versions of the negative-sign $2\pi$ Fourier transform; [F3] and [F4] imply they are Schwartz, integrable, and have inverse $a(z)=(2\pi)^{-2d}\int e^{i\lambda\cdot z}\widehat a(\lambda)\,d\lambda$. For $\lambda=(q,p)$, define the unitary map $$ (T^\epsilon_{q,p}u)(x)=e^{iq\cdot(x+\epsilon p/2)}u(x+\epsilon p). $$ The phase has modulus one and [F6] preserves the norm under translation, so $T^\epsilon_{q,p}$ is unitary, with inverse given by reversing the translation and phase. Fourier inversion [F4], this formula, Fubini [F5] and the translation change of variables [F6] give the scalar form representation $$ \mathcal B_a(u,v):=(2\pi)^{-2d}\int\widehat a(\lambda)\langle T^\epsilon_\lambda u,v\rangle\,d\lambda . $$ For $u,v\in L^2$, this scalar integral is absolutely convergent and bounded by $(2\pi)^{-2d}\|\widehat a\|_1\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$. For Schwartz $u,v$, use $T^\epsilon_{q,p}u(x)=e^{iq\cdot(x+\epsilon p/2)}u(x+\epsilon p)$, set $y=x+\epsilon p$, and then apply Fourier inversion in $q$: $\int e^{iq\cdot(x+y)/2}\widehat a(q,(y-x)/\epsilon)\,dq=(2\pi)^d\int e^{-i(y-x)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a((x+y)/2,\xi)\,d\xi$. This gives $\mathcal B_a(u,v)=\langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,v\rangle$. Both forms are bounded on $L^2\times L^2$, so [F7] extends their equality from the dense Schwartz subspace to all $L^2$ pairs; [F2] supplies the bounded Weyl extension.

Direct substitution in $T^\epsilon_{q,p}T^\epsilon_{q',p'}u$ gives the Weyl relation $$ T^\epsilon_\lambda T^\epsilon_\mu=e^{-i\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}T^\epsilon_{\lambda+\mu}. $$ For $u,v\in L^2$, first apply [step 1.1] with $w=\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)u$; then $$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)u,v\rangle =(2\pi)^{-2d}\int\widehat a(\lambda)\langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)u,T_\lambda^{\epsilon *}v\rangle\,d\lambda. $$ Apply [step 1.1] for $b$ to each pair $(u,T_\lambda^{\epsilon *}v)$. Since $T_\lambda^\epsilon$ is unitary, $\langle T_\mu^\epsilon u,T_\lambda^{\epsilon *}v\rangle=\langle T_\lambda^\epsilon T_\mu^\epsilon u,v\rangle$; the double integral is absolutely convergent with majorant $(2\pi)^{-4d}\|\widehat a\|_1\|\widehat b\|_1\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$, so Fubini and the Weyl relation give $$ c_\epsilon(z)=(2\pi)^{-4d}\iint\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)e^{i(\lambda+\mu)\cdot z}e^{-i\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}\,d\lambda\,d\mu . $$ The phase-space Fourier coefficient of $\{a,b\}$ is $-\sigma(\lambda,\mu)\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)$; this follows by differentiating the Fourier modes in the explicitly fixed Poisson convention.

Taylor's formula with integral remainder gives $$ e^{-i\epsilon\sigma/2}=1-\frac{i\epsilon\sigma}{2} -\frac{\epsilon^2\sigma^2}{4}\int_0^1(1-s)e^{-is\epsilon\sigma/2}\,ds. $$ Set $$ R_\epsilon(\lambda,\mu):=\frac{\sigma(\lambda,\mu)^2}{4} \int_0^1(1-s)e^{-is\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}\,ds . $$ Consequently the symbol remainder is $$ r_\epsilon(z)=-(2\pi)^{-4d}\iint\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)e^{i(\lambda+\mu)\cdot z}R_\epsilon(\lambda,\mu)\,d\lambda\,d\mu. $$ For multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$ with $|\alpha|,|\beta|\le K:=4d+4$, differentiate $|\alpha|$ times in $z$ and integrate by parts $|\beta|$ times in $\lambda$ to estimate $z^\beta\partial_z^\alpha r_\epsilon(z)$. Each $\lambda$-derivative of the remainder factor is bounded by $$ |\partial_\lambda^\gamma R_\epsilon(\lambda,\mu)|\le C_\gamma\langle\lambda\rangle^2\langle\mu\rangle^{|\gamma|+2} \quad (|\gamma|\le K), $$ because $\sigma$ is bilinear, $\partial_\lambda\sigma$ is linear in $\mu$, and $0<\epsilon\le1$. Derivatives of $e^{i(\lambda+\mu)\cdot z}$ contribute powers of $\lambda+\mu$. Thus the absolute integrand is bounded by a finite sum of $$ |\partial_\lambda^\gamma\widehat a(\lambda)|\,\langle\lambda\rangle^{K+2}\, |\widehat b(\mu)|\,\langle\mu\rangle^{2K+2}. $$ For completeness, in Fourier dimension $n=2d$, if $2k>L+n$, then $$ \int\langle\lambda\rangle^L|\partial^\gamma\widehat f(\lambda)|\,d\lambda \le C\sum_{|\delta|\le2k}\|\partial^\delta(z^\gamma f)\|_{L^1} \le C p_M(f) $$ whenever $M\ge2k$ and $M>|\gamma|+n$: apply $(1-\Delta_z)^k$ to $z^\gamma f$, use its Fourier multiplier $\langle\lambda\rangle^{2k}$, and integrate the resulting $\langle z\rangle^{-M+|\gamma|}$ bound. Taking $K=4d+4$, $L_a=K+2$, $L_b=2K+2$, choose $k_a=3d+4$ for $a$ and $k_b=5d+6$ for $b$. Then $2k_a>L_a+2d$, $2k_b>L_b+2d$, and $M=12d+16$ exceeds both $2k_b$ and $K+2d$, so the weighted estimates hold for all indicated derivatives. This proves $p_K(r_\epsilon)\le C_dp_M(a)p_M(b)$, uniformly in $\epsilon$. The same argument with any fixed larger $K$ proves every Schwartz seminorm of $r_\epsilon$ is finite, so $r_\epsilon\in\mathcal S$. Hence $c_\epsilon=ab+\frac{i\epsilon}{2}\{a,b\}+\epsilon^2r_\epsilon$ is Schwartz, and the weak Fourier representation from step 1.1 identifies the product in step 2.1 with $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(c_\epsilon)$.

The kernel of $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_\epsilon)$, in $q=(x+y)/2$, $s=x-y$, is $$ K_\epsilon(q,s)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{is\cdot\xi/\epsilon}r_\epsilon(q,\xi)\,d\xi. $$ Since $K=4d+4\ge2d+2$, $\langle(q,\xi)\rangle^K\ge\langle q\rangle^{d+1}\langle\xi\rangle^{d+1}$ and $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\langle\xi\rangle^{-d-1}d\xi<\infty$ imply $\int|\partial_\xi^\gamma r_\epsilon(q,\xi)|\,d\xi\le C_dp_K(r_\epsilon)\langle q\rangle^{-d-1}$ for $|\gamma|\le2d+2$. Integrating by parts with $(1-\Delta_\xi)^{d+1}$ and using this bound gives $$ |K_\epsilon(q,s)|\leq C_dp_{12d+16}(a)p_{12d+16}(b)\epsilon^{-d} \langle q\rangle^{-d-1}(1+|s|/\epsilon)^{-2d-2}. $$ For fixed $x$, $dy=2^d\,dq$ and $s=2(x-q)$, so integrating this bound in $y$ is at most a constant times $\epsilon^{-d}\int(1+|x-q|/\epsilon)^{-2d-2}\,dq\leq C_d$; the same bound holds with $x,y$ interchanged. The integral-kernel Schur estimate, proved by Cauchy–Schwarz and the row/column bounds, gives $\|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_\epsilon)\|\leq C_dp_{12d+16}(a)p_{12d+16}(b)$. Combining steps 2.1–4.1 proves the asserted Weyl composition formula with the plus sign fixed by $[Q_j,P_k]=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}$.

derivations.claim: Since $a$ is compactly supported and smooth, Fourier inversion in its $\xi$ variable identifies $K_{\epsilon,a}((x+y)/2,x-y)$ with the kernel of $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)$. Its derivatives have rapid decay in $x-y$, uniformly on compact sets of $(x+y)/2$, by [F3]. Multiplication by $V$, which has at most quadratic growth because its Hessian is bounded, and differentiation therefore preserve Schwartz vectors. Thus the commutator in the Statement is well defined on $\mathcal S$.

Write $q=(x+y)/2$ and $r=x-y$. Then $\partial_x=\frac12\partial_q+\partial_r$, $\partial_y=\frac12\partial_q-\partial_r$, so $\partial_x^2-\partial_y^2=2\partial_q\cdot\partial_r$. Acting with the kinetic operator on the two kernel variables gives $[-\epsilon^2\Delta/2,\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)]$ kernel $-\epsilon^2\partial_q\cdot\partial_rK_{\epsilon,a}$. Since $\partial_{r_j}e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}=i\xi_j e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}/\epsilon$, multiplication by $i/\epsilon$ turns this exactly into the Weyl kernel with symbol $\xi\cdot\nabla_xa$.

The potential part has kernel $(V(q+r/2)-V(q-r/2))K_{\epsilon,a}(q,r)$. Taylor's formula with integral remainder, applied to $s\mapsto V(q+sr)$ at $s=0$ on the symmetric interval $[-1/2,1/2]$, gives $$ V(q+r/2)-V(q-r/2)=r\cdot
abla V(q)+\Delta_V(q,r), $$ $$ \Delta_V(q,r)= rac1{16}\int_0^1(1-s)^2\left(D^3V(q+sr/2)[r,r,r]+D^3V(q-sr/2)[r,r,r]ight)\,ds . $$ Integration by parts in $\xi$ gives $\int e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}r_j a(q,\xi)\,d\xi=i\epsilon\int e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}\partial_{\xi_j}a(q,\xi)\,d\xi$. Therefore the linear term, multiplied by $i/\epsilon$, is the Weyl kernel with symbol $-
abla_\xi a\cdot
abla V$. Together with step 2.1 this is exactly $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(\{a,h\})$.

The kernel $K_{\epsilon,a}(q,r)$ is compactly supported in $q$ and Schwartz in $r$, since $a\in C_c^\infty$. Taylor's formula and the bounded higher derivatives of $V$ show that $\Delta_V(q,r)$ and all its $q,r$ derivatives grow at most polynomially in $r$, uniformly for $q$ in that compact set. Hence $G(q,r):=\Delta_V(q,r)K_{\epsilon,a}(q,r)$ is Schwartz in $(q,r)$; its inverse partial Fourier transform is Schwartz by [F3], and Fourier inversion [F4] recovers $G$. Define the remainder symbol by that inverse partial Fourier transform: $$ r_{\epsilon,a,V}(q,\eta):=\frac{i}{\epsilon^3}\int e^{-ir\cdot\eta/\epsilon}\Delta_V(q,r)K_{\epsilon,a}(q,r)\,dr . $$ By construction its Weyl kernel is $i\epsilon^{-3}\Delta_V(q,r)K_{\epsilon,a}(q,r)$, so the remaining potential commutator kernel, after multiplication by $i/\epsilon$, is $\epsilon^2$ times that kernel. With $r=\epsilon s$, the formula becomes $$ r_{\epsilon,a,V}(q,\eta)=i(2\pi)^{-d}\int e^{-is\cdot\eta}\frac{\Delta_V(q,\epsilon s)}{\epsilon^3}\left(\int e^{is\cdot\xi}a(q,\xi)\,d\xi\right)ds . $$ Taylor's integral formula shows $|\partial_q^\alpha\Delta_V(q,\epsilon s)|\leq C_{\alpha,V}\epsilon^3|s|^3$: differentiating in $q$ differentiates $V$, and every resulting third derivative of $V$ is bounded by hypothesis. Derivatives in $\eta$ insert powers of $s$; derivatives in $q$ of the partial Fourier transform insert derivatives of $a$. Integration by parts in $\xi$ gives decay factor $(1+|s|^2)^{-4d-5}$, uniformly in $q$, because $a$ is compactly supported in $(q,\xi)$. For $|\alpha|\le N_d$, the largest remaining radial power is $|s|^{N_d+3}=|s|^{4d+7}$; after including the $d$-dimensional radial measure, the tail is bounded by a constant times $\int_1^\infty \rho^{-3d-4}d\rho<\infty$. More explicitly, bounding all $q,\eta$ derivatives of total order at most $N_d$ uses $(1-\Delta_\xi)^{4d+5}$ on $a$, hence at most $N_d+8d+10=12d+14$ derivatives, within $M_d=12d+16$. This proves the stated uniform derivative bound.

Apply [F2] to $r_{\epsilon,a,V}$. Its bounded derivatives through $N_d$, established in step 4.1, imply $\|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a,V})\|\leq C_{d,V}p_{M_d}(a)$, uniformly for $0<\epsilon\leq1$. Combining steps 2.1, 3.1, and 4.1 proves the commutator identity on $\mathcal S$ and the asserted operator-norm bound on its remainder.

Let U⊂R^n be open and Y:U→R^n be C¹. There is a unique maximal flow Φ on an open domain
D⊂R×U containing {0}×U, and Φ is jointly C¹. Its time slices are local C¹
diffeomorphisms with inverse Φ_{−t}; $\partial_t\Phi=Y(\Phi)$ and $D_p\Phi$ is the
unique solution V of $V′=DY(\Phi)V$, V(0)=I. Each regular point has a C¹ flow box. If Y
is C², Φ and those flow boxes are C²; the second state variation W satisfies
$W′=DY(\Phi)W+D²Y(\Phi)[Ve_i,Ve_j]$, W(0)=0. Individual trajectories of a C¹ field are
C² in time. A trajectory remaining in a compact K⊂⊂U cannot have a finite maximal
endpoint. These Euclidean conclusions use no full AC or DC.

$$H(q,p)=U(q)+\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p,\qquad F(q,p)=(M^{-1}p,-\nabla U(q)).$$
Assume Countable Choice. Call this vector field **complete** when the solution through every $(q,p)$ exists for all $t\in\mathbb R$. If $F$ is complete, it has a unique global $C^1$ flow $\Phi_t$, which conserves $H$ and satisfies
$$\det D\Phi_t(q,p)=1\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$
Thus it preserves phase-space Lebesgue volume. Completeness is an explicit hypothesis. In particular, if $\nabla U$ is globally $L$-Lipschitz, then $F$ is globally Lipschitz with constant $C=\max\{\|M^{-1}\|_F,L\}$, so the global-existence and stability corollaries apply and
$$\|\Phi_t(z)-\Phi_t(w)\|_2\le e^{C|t|}\|z-w\|_2.$$

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

complex Hilbert space, let $Y$ be a dense linear subspace of $H$ that is itself
a Hilbert space continuously embedded in $H$ (for instance $Y=D(A_0)$ with the
graph norm of a self-adjoint $A_0$), let $T>0$, and let $A(t)$ for
$t\in[0,T]$ be an operator with $D(A(t))=Y$, self-adjoint as an operator on $H$,
such that $t\mapsto A(t)$ belongs to $C^1([0,T];\mathcal B(Y,H))$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). Put $L:=\sup_t\|A'(t)\|_{\mathcal B(Y,H)}$.

$U(t,s)$, $0\le s\le t\le T$, of unitary operators on $H$ with:
$U(s,s)=I$; $U(t,s)U(s,r)=U(t,r)$; $(t,s)\mapsto U(t,s)\xi$ continuous on
$\{s\le t\}$ for each $\xi\in H$; $U(t,s)Y=Y$ with
$\|U(t,s)y\|_Y\le C_T\|y\|_Y$ for a constant $C_T$ independent of
$(s,t)\in[0,T]^2$; and for every $y\in Y$ the map $t\mapsto U(t,s)y$ is $C^1$

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The bounded Hessian and [F3] imply that $\nabla V$ is globally Lipschitz. Thus $X$ is globally Lipschitz; [F2] gives a unique global flow $\Phi_t$. The bound $|X(z)|\le C(1+|z|)$ follows from this Lipschitz estimate and $X(0)$, so the integral equation and Gronwall bound $\Phi_t(z)$ on each compact time interval and compact initial set. To obtain the smoothness needed below, start with the $C^2$ flow and variational equations of [F1]. Assume inductively that the state derivatives through order $k-1$ are continuous. For a coordinate vector $e_j$, take the difference quotient of the integral equation for $D^{k-1}\Phi_t(z)$ between $z+he_j$ and $z$. The mean-value integral formula applied to each occurrence of $D^\ell X(\Phi_t(z+he_j))-D^\ell X(\Phi_t(z))$ writes this quotient as a linear integral equation whose coefficients converge uniformly on compact time/initial sets, since the lower derivatives of $\Phi$ and the derivatives of $X$ are uniformly continuous on their compact images. The chain rule expresses its limiting inhomogeneous term as
$$ \sum_{\substack{\pi\text{ a partition of }\{1,\ldots,k\}\\|\pi|\ge2}} D^{|\pi|}X(\Phi_t(z)) \big[D^{|B_1|}\Phi_t(z),\ldots,D^{|B_{|\pi|}|}\Phi_t(z)\big], $$
where $B_1,\ldots,B_{|\pi|}$ are the blocks of $\pi$; the unknown $D^k\Phi_t$ appears linearly with coefficient $DX(\Phi_t)$, and its initial value is $0$ for $k\ge2$. The corresponding linear Volterra equation has a unique solution by the same local Picard iteration as [F1], and Gronwall [F7] makes the difference between the quotient and that solution tend uniformly to zero. Thus $D^k\Phi_t$ exists and is continuous, completing the induction. Since $DX$ is bounded and all $D^\ell X$ for $\ell\ge2$ are bounded by the assumed bounds on derivatives of $V$, the variational equation bounds $D\Phi_t$; each higher equation has bounded forcing made from lower derivatives, so induction and Gronwall bound every $D^k\Phi_t$ on compact time/initial sets. Hence $(t,z)\mapsto\Phi_t(z)$ is smooth with all finite derivatives bounded there.

For $b\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{2d})$, its Weyl kernel is Schwartz in $(x,y)$. Differentiating under its integral and multiplying by powers of $x$ leaves absolutely integrable products of Schwartz functions, so $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)$ maps $\mathcal S$ into itself. Apply [F5] on $\mathcal S$ to obtain the bounded identity
$$ \frac{i}{\epsilon}[H_\epsilon,\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)] =\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(\{b,h\})+\epsilon^2\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,b,V}). $$
The right side is bounded by [F5] and [F6]. Because $\mathcal S$ is a graph core for $H_\epsilon$, this commutator identity extends to $D(H_\epsilon)$: if $u_n\in\mathcal S$, $u_n\to u$, and $H_\epsilon u_n\to H_\epsilon u$, then boundedness of $\operatorname{Op}(b)$ and of the commutator makes both $\operatorname{Op}(b)u_n$ and $H_\epsilon\operatorname{Op}(b)u_n=\operatorname{Op}(b)H_\epsilon u_n+[H_\epsilon,\operatorname{Op}(b)]u_n$ converge; closedness of $H_\epsilon$ gives $\operatorname{Op}(b)u\in D(H_\epsilon)$ and the identity there.

Put $a_s=a\circ\Phi_{t-s}$ for fixed $t$. Since $\Phi_\tau$ is a global diffeomorphism with inverse $\Phi_{-\tau}$, $\operatorname{supp}(a_s)=\Phi_{-(t-s)}(\operatorname{supp}a)$. Thus $a_s\in C_c^\infty$, its supports lie in one compact set for $|s|,|t|\le T$, and every fixed finite symbol seminorm of $a_s$ is uniformly bounded. To verify the bracket identity, write $X=(\partial_\xi h,-\partial_x h)$, so $Xf=\{f,h\}$. Differentiating the autonomous flow law $\Phi_{\tau+r}(z)=\Phi_\tau(\Phi_r(z))$ in $r$ at $0$ gives $D\Phi_\tau(z)X(z)=X(\Phi_\tau(z))$. The chain rule now gives
$$ \partial_s a_s=-\{a_s,h\}. $$
The family $H_\epsilon/\epsilon$ is constant on the common graph domain $D(H_\epsilon)$, so [F4] supplies the forward propagator for $t\ge0$; its inverse defines $U_\epsilon(t)=U_\epsilon(-t)^*$ for $t<0$. It preserves $D(H_\epsilon)$ and is strongly differentiable there.

For $\psi\in D(H_\epsilon)$, differentiate
$$ F(s)\psi:=U_\epsilon(s)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a_s)U_\epsilon(s)\psi . $$
The domain preservation in [F4] and step 1.2 justify the product rule in $L^2$; the symbol derivative in step 2.1 is also an operator-norm derivative by [F6], since the symbols and their difference quotients have common compact support and converge with all derivatives required by that estimate. The two Hamiltonian terms combine to $U_\epsilon(s)^*(i/\epsilon)[H_\epsilon,\operatorname{Op}(a_s)]U_\epsilon(s)$; $\partial_s\operatorname{Op}(a_s)=-\operatorname{Op}(\{a_s,h\})$ cancels its Poisson term by step 1.2. $$ F'(s)\psi=\epsilon^2U_\epsilon(s)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a_s,V})U_\epsilon(s)\psi . $$
Step 2.1 gives a uniform bound on $p_{12d+16}(a_s)$. The remainder estimate [F5] followed by [F6] consequently yields
$$ \sup_{|s|,|t|\le T}\|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a_s,V})\|\le C_{T,V,a}. $$
Integrate the derivative by [F7], use unitarity, and evaluate the endpoints $F(t)\psi=U_\epsilon(t)^*\operatorname{Op}(a)U_\epsilon(t)\psi$ and $F(0)\psi=\operatorname{Op}(a\circ\Phi_t)\psi$. If $V$ has degree at most two, then $D^3V=0$, so the integral Taylor remainder $\Delta_V$ in the proof of [[lem-nrqmx-cubic-moyal-commutator-remainder]] vanishes. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space, let $Y$ be a dense linear subspace of $H$ that is itself
a Hilbert space continuously embedded in $H$ (for instance $Y=D(A_0)$ with the
graph norm of a self-adjoint $A_0$), let $T>0$, and let $A(t)$ for
$t\in[0,T]$ be an operator with $D(A(t))=Y$, self-adjoint as an operator on $H$,
such that $t\mapsto A(t)$ belongs to $C^1([0,T];\mathcal B(Y,H))$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). Put $L:=\sup_t\|A'(t)\|_{\mathcal B(Y,H)}$.
Then:

(a) *Existence and uniqueness of a strong propagator.* There is a family
$U(t,s)$, $0\le s\le t\le T$, of unitary operators on $H$ with:
$U(s,s)=I$; $U(t,s)U(s,r)=U(t,r)$; $(t,s)\mapsto U(t,s)\xi$ continuous on
$\{s\le t\}$ for each $\xi\in H$; $U(t,s)Y=Y$ with
$\|U(t,s)y\|_Y\le C_T\|y\|_Y$ for a constant $C_T$ independent of
$(s,t)\in[0,T]^2$; and for every $y\in Y$ the map $t\mapsto U(t,s)y$ is $C^1$
in $H$ with
$$i\,\partial_tU(t,s)y=A(t)U(t,s)y,\qquad s\le t\le T.$$

(b) *Uniqueness.* If $V(t,s)$ is another family of bounded linear operators on $H$ with the same strong equation
on $Y$, $V(s,s)=I$ and $\sup_{r}\|V(r,s)y\|_{H}<\infty$, then $V=U$.

(c) *Equations for the reverse and adjoint.* $U(t,s)Y=Y$ for all $0\le s\le t\le T$
and $U(s,t):=U(t,s)^{-1}$ satisfies $i\partial_sU(s,t)y=A(s)U(s,t)y$ for
$y\in Y$; $U(t,s)^*=U(s,t)$. Equivalently, differentiating the second
argument of the forward propagator gives $i\partial_sU(t,s)y=-U(t,s)A(s)y$.
The domain maps are jointly strongly continuous in $Y$.

The theorem is stated for the abstract family $A$; a physical generator is
obtained by $A=H_{\mathrm{energy}}/\hbar$ after choosing a time unit.

(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, $\epsilon>0$, $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, and $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $\|u\|_2=1$. With the definitions of [def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner], the Wigner distribution $W_\epsilon[u]$ is real and integrable, and

$$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,u\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}a(x,\xi)W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx\,d\xi , $$

$$ \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,d\xi=|u(x)|^2,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx=|(\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi)|^2. $$

The Wigner distribution need not be nonnegative.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $0<\epsilon\le1$, and $V\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ with every partial derivative of total order at least $2$ bounded. Set
$$ h(x,\xi)=\frac{|\xi|^2}{2}+V(x),\qquad H_\epsilon^0=-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\Delta+V(x)\quad\text{on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d). $$
Assume, as an explicit operator hypothesis, that for each $\epsilon$ a self-adjoint operator $H_\epsilon$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_\epsilon^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for $H_\epsilon$. Let
$$ U_\epsilon(t)=U_\epsilon(t,0) $$
be the unitary propagator supplied by [[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-common-domain-nonautonomous-evolution]] for the constant generator $H_\epsilon/\epsilon$. Define the global Hamiltonian flow by
$$ \dot x=\xi,\qquad \dot\xi=-\nabla V(x),\qquad \Phi_0=I. $$
For every $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and finite $T>0$, there is $C_{T,V,a}<\infty$, independent of $0<\epsilon\le1$, such that
$$ \sup_{|t|\le T} \left\|U_\epsilon(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_\epsilon(t) -\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t)\right\|_{L^2\to L^2} \le C_{T,V,a}\epsilon^2. $$
Only fixed finite times are covered. No Ehrenfest-time, caustic-uniformity, or physical measurement conclusion is asserted. If $V$ is a polynomial of degree at most two, the difference is identically zero.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Assume countable choice. For complex $C^1$ functions $u,v$ on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, Lebesgue integration gives $\int_a^b u'v=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^b uv'$ and $\int_a^b u'=u(b)-u(a)$. If instead $u,v\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, $u'v,uv'\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and $u(x)v(x)\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, then $\int_{\mathbb R}u'v=-\int_{\mathbb R}uv'$.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

derivations.claim:
The scaled oscillator eigenfunctions are polynomial multiples of $e^{-x^2/(2\epsilon)}$. To verify the core hypothesis of [[thm-nrqmx-quadratic-egorov]], take $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ and set $L f=-\epsilon^2f''/2+x^2f/2\in L^2$. Integration by parts against each Hermite eigenfunction $\psi_n^\epsilon$, whose polynomial-Gaussian tails make the endpoint products vanish, gives
$$ \langle Lf,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle =\langle f,L\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle =\epsilon(n+\tfrac12)\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle. $$
Parseval for the complete basis [F1] yields
$$ \sum_{n\ge0}\epsilon^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle|^2 =\|Lf\|_2^2<\infty. $$
Thus $f\in D(H_\epsilon)$. The coefficients of $H_\epsilon f$ in the Hermite basis are $\epsilon(n+\tfrac12)\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle$, the same coefficients as $Lf$; completeness of that basis gives $H_\epsilon f=Lf$. The finite Hermite span is contained in $\mathcal S$ and is a graph core by [F1]; since $\mathcal S\subset D(H_\epsilon)$, $\mathcal S$ is also a core. This checks every operator hypothesis of [F4].

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $0<\epsilon\le1$, and $V\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ with every partial derivative of total order at least $2$ bounded. Set

$$ U_\epsilon(t)=U_\epsilon(t,0) $$
be the unitary propagator supplied by [[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-common-domain-nonautonomous-evolution]] for the constant generator $H_\epsilon/\epsilon$. Define the global Hamiltonian flow by
$$ \dot x=\xi,\qquad \dot\xi=-\nabla V(x),\qquad \Phi_0=I. $$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Write $A^2=2\epsilon^{-1}(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2}$. The product in the Wigner integrand is $$ \psi^\epsilon_1(x+y/2)\overline{\psi^\epsilon_1(x-y/2)} =A^2\left(x^2-\frac{y^2}{4}\right) e^{-x^2/\epsilon-y^2/(4\epsilon)}. $$ By [F4], $G_\epsilon''(\xi)=\int(-y^2/\epsilon^2)e^{-y^2/(4\epsilon)}e^{-iy\xi/\epsilon}dy$. Differentiating the explicit Gaussian in [F3] gives $$ \int y^2e^{-y^2/(4\epsilon)}e^{-iy\xi/\epsilon}dy =-\epsilon^2G_\epsilon''(\xi) =(2\epsilon-4\xi^2)G_\epsilon(\xi). $$ Substitution in the Wigner definition [F2] therefore yields $$ W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_1](x,\xi) =(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1}A^2e^{-x^2/\epsilon} \left(x^2G_\epsilon(\xi)-\frac14(2\epsilon-4\xi^2)G_\epsilon(\xi)\right) =\frac1{\pi\epsilon} \left(\frac{2(x^2+\xi^2)}{\epsilon}-1\right) e^{-(x^2+\xi^2)/\epsilon}. $$ Every factor and sign follows from the displayed negative-sign Fourier convention.

The exponential and the prefactor $1/(\pi\epsilon)$ are strictly positive. Thus $W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_1](x,\xi)<0$ exactly when $2(x^2+\xi^2)/\epsilon-1<0$, which is the disk $x^2+\xi^2<\epsilon/2$. This normalized pure state refutes universal Wigner nonnegativity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
